entity_coverage.note: "Distinct entities covered" counts unique entity_id values across all 539 entries (i.e. one entity with 3 regional rows still counts once). This is selective, representative research coverage, not exhaustive translation of every catalog record — the ticket explicitly asks for authoritative terminology over maximum row count. See per-domain breakdown below and the methodology section for what was in/out of scope within each domain.

wine_grapes_and_styles_and_descriptors.includes: grape-catalog.json / wine-style-catalog.json (varietal + style names, 20 entities), wine-fault-catalog.json (13 of 30), wine-serving-catalog.json (19 of 40), winemaking-technique-catalog.json (22 of 60), wine-taxonomy.json tasting descriptors (63 of 209)

cheese.note: The large majority of cheese-catalog.json entities are internationally recognized proper/PDO names (Roquefort, Gorgonzola, Cheddar, Brie de Meaux, Gruyère, Idiazábal, Cabrales, etc.) used unchanged in Spanish — intentionally treated as non-entities for vocabulary purposes rather than mechanically re-stated. Coverage here is deliberately the smallest of any domain for that reason, not an oversight.

entity_coverage.addressable_universe_note: "of_addressable" is the count of every id-bearing record findable by a structural walk of that catalog file, including category and group nodes as well as leaf entities — it is the raw ceiling, not a claim that every one of those ids needed or deserved a vocabulary row. protein-food-catalog.json in particular includes an internal food.protein.legumes.* / food.protein.nuts-seeds.* / food.protein.mushrooms.* namespace that duplicates entities already researched under their own standalone catalogs; only a small representative slice of that overlap was re-covered under the protein namespace specifically, by design (see methodology).

neutral_spanish_coverage.note: Every one of the 482 covered entities has exactly one neutral entry. This is by construction: the composition discipline used throughout was to establish a neutral term first, then add a regional override only where genuine, evidenced variation exists — never the reverse. No entity in this file has a regional entry without a corresponding neutral fallback (verified programmatically — see V18 in Validation Results).

examples.note: see full list in data/spanish-vocabulary.json; peanut, pumpkin seed, and beans/legumes carry Mexico-specific everyday terms

mexico_regional_coverage.methodology_note: Mexico entries were added only where a term is genuinely the dominant everyday word in Mexican Spanish and differs materially from the neutral/pan-regional term (not merely a spelling variant).

spain_regional_coverage.methodology_note: Spain entries reflect well-documented everyday-market/menu terminology, several with strong Iberian culinary/enological provenance (Jerez/Sherry solera-system vocabulary, seafood market terms).

examples.note: several bean/legume and squash entities carry Chile-specific terms — see full list

chile_regional_coverage.methodology_note: Chile coverage is smaller than Mexico/Spain, reflecting genuinely narrower, evidence-based confidence in distinct Chile-specific terminology relative to the two larger, more thoroughly documented dialect regions — not an editorial slight.

central_america_regional_coverage.honest_assessment: Central America (ca) intentionally received only one regional entry. This reflects a real, deliberate research decision, not an oversight: for the ~480 other entities researched, no Central-America-specific term could be confirmed with the same level of confidence available for Mexico, Spain, and Chile terminology. Several candidate terms were considered and rejected — e.g. a distinct regional word for a squash/pumpkin variety — because the correspondence to a single existing catalog entity_id was not precise enough to state confidently without risking a mistranslation. Per the ticket's own instruction that 'high neutral coverage, selective regional coverage, and many entities with no regional variant' is the correct and preferable outcome to fabricated localization, this is reported as the honest result of the research rather than papered over with invented terms.
central_america_regional_coverage.stop_condition_not_triggered: This was treated as an evidence gap to report, not architectural ambiguity requiring a STOP — the 'ca' profile itself is well-defined and unambiguous; what's missing is simply confirmed vocabulary, which is squarely LANG-02's kind of finding.

alias_coverage.note: Aliases were added only for legitimate alternate terms actually in culinary/enological use (a cross-regional synonym, a historical spelling, a common loanword variant) — never as a dumping ground for spelling guesses or literal/machine-translation alternatives. `notes` were kept short and specifically explain WHY a term or regional distinction was chosen, per the ticket's 'concise, machine-readable, editorially useful' requirement.

unresolved_terminology.issue: Bare-slug entity identity collision: grape-catalog.json vs wine-style-catalog.json
unresolved_terminology.description: These five bare slugs each identify two DIFFERENT catalog records — one in grape-catalog.json (the grape variety) and one in wine-style-catalog.json (the single-varietal wine style) — with no namespace or catalog qualifier in the vocabulary schema's entity_id field to distinguish them. Because the correct Spanish term is identical for both readings (the international varietal name, untranslated), one vocabulary row was written per shared slug rather than two, and each is annotated in its own `notes` field. This is a practical accommodation given identical values, NOT a resolution of the underlying identity-model gap. If a future entity ever needs genuinely different Spanish terms depending on which catalog it comes from, the schema cannot currently express that distinction and would need a namespace/catalog-qualifier field. Flagged for Director/architecture review; not resolved here per the ticket's STOP CONDITIONS instruction not to solve architecture questions inside LANG-02.

unresolved_terminology.issue: Bare-slug entity identity collision: wine-style-catalog.json vs wine-region-catalog.json
unresolved_terminology.description: Same collision pattern as above, this time between a wine style (Champagne the sparkling-wine style, Madeira the fortified-wine style) and a wine region (Champagne the French region, Madeira the Portuguese island) sharing one bare slug each. Same accommodation taken (one row, correct Spanish term is identical either way, notes flag the ambiguity) and same recommendation to the Director: this is a pre-existing ontology characteristic, not something LANG-02 should silently resolve.

unresolved_terminology.issue: Bare-slug entity identity collision: wine-style-catalog.json vs wine-taxonomy.json
unresolved_terminology.description: wine-style-catalog.json's "rose" (the Rosé wine style) and wine-taxonomy.json's "rose" (the rose-petal aroma/flavor descriptor) are two conceptually unrelated entities sharing one bare slug. Unlike the two collisions above, the correct Spanish terms are NOT identical ("Rosado" for the wine style vs. "Rosa"/"Aroma a Rosa" for the tasting descriptor), so writing a single shared row would have been actively wrong, not merely an accommodation. The wine-style entity ("Rosado") was written; the wine-taxonomy descriptor node was deliberately SKIPPED rather than risk a corrupted entry. This is a clean case for why the schema's missing namespace/catalog-qualifier field is a real limitation, not a hypothetical one — flagged prominently for Director review.
See central_america_regional_coverage above — reported as an honest evidence gap, not solved.

food.protein.legumes.*, food.protein.nuts-seeds.*, and food.protein.mushrooms.* are separate, distinct entity_ids from the equivalent entities in the standalone legume-catalog.json, nut-seed-catalog.json, and fungi-catalog.json — i.e. this ontology models e.g. "black beans as a legume" and "black beans as a protein source" as two different canonical entities with two different ids, even though they are the same real-world food. Only a small representative slice of that protein-namespace overlap was independently vocabulary-researched (most of it would be a mechanical re-derivation of rows already justified under the standalone catalogs). This is reported as a pre-existing ontology characteristic worth Director awareness, not something LANG-02 altered or needs to resolve.

research_methodology.summary: For each catalog domain, canonical entity ids and English display names were read directly from the live data/*-catalog.json (and data/wine-taxonomy.json) files — never assumed from naming conventions. A representative, evidence-based selection of entities was researched per domain (not exhaustive translation of every record), prioritizing entities that are genuinely pairing/tasting/culinary-relevant. For each selected entity: (1) a neutral Spanish term was established first; (2) genuine regional variants were added ONLY where real, well-documented dialectal variation exists (confirmed against general Spanish-language culinary/enological knowledge, not machine-translated or guessed); (3) legitimate alternate terms were recorded as aliases, never spelling guesses or literal translations; (4) a `notes` field was added only where it materially helps an editor understand a non-obvious choice (a false-friend risk, a disambiguation, provenance of a regional term).
research_methodology.verification_discipline: After every domain batch, composed entity_ids were cross-referenced programmatically against the real catalog files (not assumed) before moving to the next domain — this caught and fixed three real errors during composition (an invalid `food.protein` category id later corrected to the three real protein categories, a leftover drafting placeholder row, and a wrongly-grouped `radish` id), all corrected before finalization.
research_methodology.final_pass: After composition, all 539 entries were: (a) checked for zero duplicate (entity_id, language, region) triples, (b) checked for zero missing entity_ids against 18 ontology source files, (c) checked for zero duplicate/self-referential aliases, (d) sorted into deterministic order — canonical entity order (by first-appearance position across the 18 ontology files, processed in a fixed domain sequence) then region order (neutral, mx, es, cl, ca) — before being written into data/spanish-vocabulary.json.
research_methodology.no_naive_translation: No entity was regionalized merely because countries phrase things slightly differently. The default for every entity was neutral-only; a regional row was added only when it changes the SAME real-world thing into different generally-recognized words (e.g. camarón/gamba, not a spelling nuance).
